item.title: Extracting Data from OpenStreetMap
item.description:
Introduction

OpenStreetMap (OSM) is a free and open map of the world, built by millions of volunteers, much like Wikipedia. Anyone can use the data for any purpose, including commercial ones, as long as they credit “© OpenStreetMap contributors” and share any database they derive from it under the same Open Database License (ODbL). Every map in this post carries that credit.

Underneath the map tiles is a database of roads, buildings, shops, bus stops and much more. This post pulls the places to eat in Durham, NC out of that database, avoids a few common traps, and asks how good the data is.

This post was first written in 2020 and rewritten in 2026.

How OSM data is structured

OSM has only three kinds of objects:

  • Nodes are points with a latitude and longitude. A bench, a bus stop, or a café drawn as a single point is a node.
  • Ways are ordered lists of nodes. An open way is a line (a road, a stream); a closed way is usually an area (a building, a park).
  • Relations group other objects. A bus route, a city boundary, or a building with a courtyard is a relation.

None of these objects has a fixed “type” or attribute table. Instead, each carries a set of tags, which are key = value pairs. A restaurant might carry:

key value
amenity restaurant
name Mateo Bar de Tapas
cuisine spanish
addr:street West Chapel Hill Street
opening_hours Tu-Sa 17:00-22:00

Only the first tag says what the object is. The rest are optional, and whether they are filled in depends on whether some volunteer bothered. There is no enforced schema: tags are conventions, documented on the OSM Wiki’s Map Features page, and Taginfo shows how often each is actually used. Keys useful in planning include amenity (restaurants, schools, clinics), shop, highway (roads and bus stops), leisure (parks) and building.

We will use the Overpass API through the osmdata package, which suits a city and a handful of tags. For a whole state or country, download an extract from Geofabrik instead (the osmextract package).

A sturdier way to call Overpass

Overpass servers are run by volunteers and shared by everyone, and the main one often refuses requests when it is busy. Small queries, a fallback server, and saving every answer to disk make code that keeps working.

osmdata builds the query for us. opq_string() shows the query in Overpass’s own language:

opq(bbox = c(-78.95, 35.98, -78.88, 36.02)) |>
  add_osm_feature(key = "amenity", value = "restaurant") |>
  opq_string() |>
  cat()
# [out:xml][timeout:25];
# (
#   node ["amenity"="restaurant"] (35.98,-78.95,36.02,-78.88);
#   way ["amenity"="restaurant"] (35.98,-78.95,36.02,-78.88);
#   relation ["amenity"="restaurant"] (35.98,-78.95,36.02,-78.88);
# );
# (._;>;);
# out body;

The query asks for every node, way and relation tagged amenity = restaurant in the box, and for enough geometry to draw them.

The function below first looks for a saved answer to the same query on disk. If there is none, it tries each server in turn and saves the answer. Either way, osmdata converts it into sf objects.

endpoints <- c("https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter",
               "https://maps.mail.ru/osm/tools/overpass/api/interpreter",
               "https://overpass.kumi.systems/api/interpreter")

cache_dir <- here::here("osm_cache")   # a folder in your project

get_osm <- function(q) {
  dir.create(cache_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  qs   <- opq_string(q)
  file <- file.path(cache_dir, paste0(rlang::hash(qs), ".osm"))   # one file per distinct query
  if (file.exists(file)) return(osmdata_sf(q, doc = file))

  for (round in 1:3) {                          # up to three passes over the servers
  for (u in endpoints) {
    resp <- request(u) |>
      req_body_form(data = qs) |>
      req_user_agent("osm-tutorial (R httr2)") |>
      req_timeout(180) |>
      req_retry(max_tries = 3, backoff = function(attempt) 30) |>   # wait 30 s between tries
      req_error(is_error = function(resp) FALSE) |>   # inspect the status ourselves
      req_perform() |>
      tryCatch(error = function(e) NULL)           # network failures return NULL
    if (!is.null(resp) && resp_status(resp) == 200) {
      writeBin(resp_body_raw(resp), file)
      return(osmdata_sf(q, doc = file))
    }
  }
  Sys.sleep(60)                                 # everyone is busy; wait a minute
  }
  stop("No Overpass server answered. Try again later.")
}

On a quiet day, osmdata_sf(q) does the same job against a single server. To get fresh data, delete the osm_cache folder in your project.

Defining the study area

getbb() asks Nominatim, OSM’s place-name search, for the location of a place. By default it returns a bounding box, the smallest rectangle around the place. With format_out = "sf_polygon" it returns the actual boundary.

durham_bb <- getbb("Durham, North Carolina")
durham_bb
#         min       max
# x -79.00750 -78.75691
# y  35.86635  36.13701

durham <- getbb("Durham, North Carolina", format_out = "sf_polygon") |>
  filter(addresstype == "city") |>
  select(name) |>
  st_make_valid()

From here on we work in North Carolina State Plane (EPSG:32119, metres), with grayed OSM tiles behind the static maps.

Basemap code 
library(maptiles)
durham_m <- st_transform(durham, 32119)

osm_tiles <- get_tiles(durham_m, provider = "OpenStreetMap", zoom = 12, crop = TRUE,
                       cachedir = cache_dir)

to_gray <- function(tiles, wash = 0.7) {   # wash = 1 keeps full contrast; smaller is paler
  gray <- 0.299 * tiles[[1]] + 0.587 * tiles[[2]] + 0.114 * tiles[[3]]   # luminance of the red, green, blue bands
  255 - (255 - gray) * wash
}
gray_basemap <- function(wash = 0.7, bbox = NULL) {   # a tmap layer to start every static map with
  tm_shape(to_gray(osm_tiles, wash), bbox = bbox) +
    tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = c("black", "white"), limits = c(0, 255)),
              col.legend = tm_legend_hide())
}

Bounding boxes are not the same as city limits.

tmap_mode("plot")
bb_poly <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(durham_m))

gray_basemap() +
  tm_shape(bb_poly) +
  tm_borders(col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = "dashed") +
  tm_shape(durham_m) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "steelblue", fill_alpha = 0.3, col = "steelblue") +
  tm_credits("© OpenStreetMap contributors", position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_title("City of Durham (blue) and its bounding box (red)") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

Whose boundary?

The boundary from Nominatim is the one drawn in OSM by volunteers. The Census Bureau publishes its own, which is the one tidycensus attaches.

library(tigris)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

durham_census <- places(state = "NC", year = 2024, cb = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE) |>
  filter(GEOID == "3719000") |>        # Durham city
  st_transform(32119) |>
  st_make_valid()

osm_b <- st_make_valid(durham_m)

only_in <- function(a, b) {   # parts of a not in b
  st_difference(st_geometry(a), st_geometry(b)) |>
    st_buffer(-20) |>          # shrink and regrow by 20 m: drops slivers from slightly
    st_buffer(20)              # different line work, keeps the real patches
}

gray_basemap() +
  tm_shape(only_in(durham_census, osm_b)) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "#7570b3", lwd = 0) +
  tm_shape(only_in(osm_b, durham_census)) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "#1b9e77", lwd = 0) +
  tm_title("Only in the Census boundary (purple) or only in OSM's (green)") +
  tm_credits("© OpenStreetMap contributors", position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

Cities annex land every year, and each source catches up on its own schedule. Use the boundary that matches the rest of your data.

Overpass works with rectangles, so we download for the box and then clip to the boundary.

Downloading food places in a loop

Restaurants are tagged amenity = restaurant. Someone interested in “places to eat” would also want fast_food, cafe, bar, pub and food_court. Instead of one large query, we send one query per value, pausing between them to be polite to the server.

food_types <- c("restaurant", "fast_food", "cafe", "bar", "pub", "food_court")

food_raw <- map(food_types, function(v) {
  Sys.sleep(2)
  opq(durham_bb, timeout = 120) |>
    add_osm_feature(key = "amenity", value = v) |>
    get_osm()
}) |>
  set_names(food_types)

food_raw$restaurant

Each result is a list of sf layers: osm_points, osm_lines, osm_polygons, osm_multilines and osm_multipolygons.

The vertex trap

If you only use osm_points, it contains every node in the result, including the corners of each building outline. Those corner nodes have no tags.

rest <- food_raw$restaurant
tibble(layer = c("osm_points: every node, including building corners",
                 "osm_points tagged amenity = restaurant",
                 "osm_polygons: restaurants drawn as building outlines",
                 "osm_multipolygons: outlines with holes or several parts"),
       n     = c(nrow(rest$osm_points),
                 sum(!is.na(rest$osm_points$amenity)),
                 nrow(rest$osm_polygons),
                 nrow(rest$osm_multipolygons %||% tibble()))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Layer", "Features"))
Layer Features
osm_points: every node, including building corners 1016
osm_points tagged amenity = restaurant 211
osm_polygons: restaurants drawn as building outlines 114
osm_multipolygons: outlines with holes or several parts 0

Counting all points would inflate the number of restaurants several times over, and the restaurants drawn as building outlines would be represented only by their corners. The right approach keeps tagged points and turns each area into a single representative point. st_point_on_surface() is better than st_centroid() here, because a centroid can fall outside an L-shaped building.

keep <- c("osm_id", "name", "amenity", "cuisine", "opening_hours",
          "addr:street", "addr:housenumber", "website", "phone")

tagged <- function(layer) {     # an empty layer has no amenity column at all
  if (is.null(layer) || !"amenity" %in% names(layer)) return(NULL)
  filter(layer, !is.na(amenity))
}

as_points <- function(x) {
  pts   <- tagged(x$osm_points)
  areas <- bind_rows(tagged(x$osm_polygons), tagged(x$osm_multipolygons))
  if (nrow(areas) > 0) {
    areas <- areas |> st_make_valid() |> st_point_on_surface()
  }
  bind_rows(pts, areas) |>
    select(any_of(keep))      # some tags are missing for some types
}

food <- map(food_raw, as_points) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  distinct(osm_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  st_filter(durham)           # clip the bounding box to the city

food |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(amenity, sort = TRUE) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("amenity", "Places"))
amenity Places
restaurant 272
fast_food 155
cafe 41
bar 34
pub 10
food_court 2

There are 514 places to eat in the city of Durham in OSM today, of which 272 are restaurants.

Exercise 1: Which boundary?

How many food places are inside Durham’s bounding box but outside the city? What share of all places in the box is that?

Hint: combine food_raw without the st_filter() step, then use st_filter() with .predicate = st_disjoint.

Solution 
food_box <- map(food_raw, as_points) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  distinct(osm_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

outside <- st_filter(food_box, durham, .predicate = st_disjoint)
tibble(in_box = nrow(food_box), outside_city = nrow(outside),
       share_outside = scales::percent(nrow(outside) / nrow(food_box))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("In the box", "Outside the city", "Share outside"))
In the box Outside the city Share outside
608 94 15%

Anything counted “per city” from a bounding box would be badly off.

Visualise the data

An interactive map

Click a point to see its tags. Notice how many have no cuisine or opening hours.

library(tmap.mapgl)   # adds the "maplibre" mode, which draws vector basemaps such as OpenFreeMap
tmap_mode("maplibre")

m_food <- tm_shape(durham) +
  tm_borders(col = "gray40", lwd = 1, group = "City limits") +
  tm_shape(food) +
  tm_dots(fill = "firebrick",
          size = 0.5,
          id = "name",
          popup = tm_popup(vars = c("amenity", "cuisine", "opening_hours", "addr:street", "website")),
          group = "Places to eat") +
  tm_basemap("ofm.positron", group = "OpenFreeMap basemap")

frameWidget(tmap_maplibre(m_food))

Density on a hexagonal grid

With hundreds of points, a dot map hides the overlap downtown. Counting points in equal-area hexagons shows where food places concentrate.

food_m <- st_transform(food, 32119)

hex <- st_make_grid(durham_m, cellsize = 800, square = FALSE) |>   # 800 m across the flats
  st_as_sf() |>
  st_filter(durham_m) |>
  mutate(hex_id = row_number())

hex$n_food <- lengths(st_intersects(hex, food_m))

The basemap supplies roads and place names. We add labels only for the places discussed below.

landmarks <- tribble(   # coordinates read off openstreetmap.org; dx, dy move the label off the cluster
  ~label,             ~lon,     ~lat,     ~dx,  ~dy,
  "Ninth Street",     -78.9232, 36.0100,   2.8,  1.1,
  "Downtown",         -78.9030, 35.9960,   3.4,  0,
  "Duke / Erwin Rd",  -78.9410, 35.9985,  -4.2,  0,
  "New Hope Commons", -78.9898, 35.9538,   4,   -1.1,
  "Southpoint",       -78.9450, 35.9030,   0,   -1.2,
  "Page Road (RTP)",  -78.8480, 35.8788,  -4.4,  0) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(32119)

tmap_mode("plot")
food_hex <- hex |>
  filter(n_food > 0) |>
  mutate(class = cut(n_food, breaks = c(0, 2, 9, 19, Inf), labels = c("1-2", "3-9", "10-19", "20+")))
food_hex$neighbours  <- lengths(st_touches(food_hex))
food_hex$to_landmark <- apply(st_distance(food_hex, landmarks), 1, min)   # metres to the nearest label

examples <- food_hex |>              # one labelled hexagon per colour, plus the outliers; no legend needed
  arrange(neighbours, desc(to_landmark)) |>
  slice_head(n = 1, by = class) |>   # an isolated hexagon away from the labels is easiest to see
  bind_rows(filter(food_hex, n_food >= 15)) |>
  distinct(hex_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(text_col = if_else(class %in% c("1-2", "3-9"), "black", "white"))

m_hex <- gray_basemap(wash = 0.35, bbox = st_bbox(food_hex)) +   # pale background, zoomed to the hexagons
  tm_shape(food_hex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "class",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = viridisLite::viridis(4, end = 0.85, direction = -1)),   # green to purple
              fill.legend = tm_legend_hide(),
              col = "white", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_shape(examples) +
  tm_text("n_food", size = 0.6, col = "text_col", col.scale = tm_scale_asis(), fontface = "bold") +
  tm_shape(landmarks) +
  tm_text("label", size = 0.75, fontface = "bold", xmod = "dx", ymod = "dy",
          bgcol = "white", bgcol_alpha = 0.7) +
  tm_credits("© OpenStreetMap contributors", position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

m_hex + tm_title("Places to eat in Durham, 800 m hexagons")

Ninth Street, next to Duke’s East Campus, is the densest cluster, followed by downtown. The rest are shopping centres at freeway interchanges: New Hope Commons where US 15-501 meets I-40, Southpoint off I-40, and the strip along Page Road near Research Triangle Park.

Exercise 2: Supermarkets

Download supermarkets (shop = supermarket) in Durham. Then, for each hexagon in hex, compute the straight-line distance from its centre to the nearest supermarket, and map it. Which parts of the city are more than 2 km from one?

Hint: st_nearest_feature() returns the index of the nearest feature; st_distance(..., by_element = TRUE) then gives the distance to it.

Solution 
supermarkets <- opq(durham_bb, timeout = 120) |>
  add_osm_feature(key = "shop", value = "supermarket") |>
  get_osm()
supermarkets <- bind_rows(
  supermarkets$osm_points |> filter(!is.na(shop)),
  bind_rows(supermarkets$osm_polygons, supermarkets$osm_multipolygons) |>
    st_make_valid() |> st_point_on_surface()) |>
  select(osm_id, name) |>
  st_transform(32119)

library(units)
hex_centres <- st_centroid(hex)
nearest <- st_nearest_feature(hex_centres, supermarkets)
hex$dist_km <- st_distance(hex_centres, supermarkets[nearest, ], by_element = TRUE) |>
  set_units(km) |>
  drop_units()                          # tmap's colour scales want plain numbers

tmap_mode("plot")
gray_basemap() +
  tm_shape(durham_m) +
  tm_borders(col = "gray30") +
  tm_shape(hex |> filter(dist_km > 2) |> st_intersection(st_geometry(durham_m))) +   # clip to the city
  tm_polygons(fill = "#6a51a3", fill_alpha = 0.55, col = "white", lwd = 0.2) +
  tm_shape(supermarkets |> st_filter(durham_m)) +
  tm_dots(fill = "black", size = 0.3) +
  tm_title("Shaded: more than 2 km in a straight line from a supermarket (black dots)", size = 0.8) +
  tm_credits("© OpenStreetMap contributors", position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

scales::percent(mean(hex$dist_km > 2))   # share of hexagons more than 2 km away
# [1] "46%"

Straight-line distance understates the real trip, and supermarkets just outside the city still count, which is why we did not clip them to the boundary.

Exercise 3: Food near transit

What share of Durham’s food places are within 400 m (about a five-minute walk) of a bus stop? Bus stops are tagged highway = bus_stop.

Solution 
bus <- opq(durham_bb, timeout = 120) |>
  add_osm_feature(key = "highway", value = "bus_stop") |>
  get_osm()
bus_stops <- bus$osm_points |>
  filter(!is.na(highway)) |>
  st_transform(32119)

food_m$near_bus <- lengths(st_is_within_distance(food_m, bus_stops, dist = 400)) > 0

food_m |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(places = n(), share_near_bus = scales::percent(mean(near_bus)), .by = amenity) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("amenity", "Places", "Within 400 m of a bus stop"))
amenity Places Within 400 m of a bus stop
restaurant 272 95%
fast_food 155 96%
cafe 41 95%
bar 34 100%
pub 10 100%
food_court 2 100%

Mapping of bus stops is uneven; GoDurham publishes its stops as GTFS, which would be a better source for real work.

How complete are the tags?

OSM is often very good at where things are and much weaker on their attributes. Before you analyse cuisine or opening hours, check how often they are filled in.

tag_cols <- c("name", "cuisine", "opening_hours", "addr:street", "website", "phone")

share_present <- function(x) {
  mean(!is.na(x))
}

completeness <- food |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(across(all_of(tag_cols), share_present)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "tag", values_to = "share")

ggplot(completeness, aes(x = share, y = fct_reorder(tag, share))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 1)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1.08)) +
  labs(x = "Share of Durham's food places with the tag", y = NULL,
       caption = "Data © OpenStreetMap contributors") +
  theme_minimal()

Names are nearly always present, because a nameless café is hard to map. Opening hours and websites are much patchier. Completeness can also vary across space, since tags depend on whether an active mapper lives nearby. An analysis that drops places with missing tags may quietly drop whole neighbourhoods; mapping the places with no opening_hours is a quick check.

Exercise 4: What cuisines?

List the ten most common cuisines among Durham’s restaurants. Some places list more than one, separated by semicolons (mexican;tex-mex); count each separately. What share of restaurants have no cuisine at all?

Hint: separate_longer_delim().

Solution 
rest_now <- food |> filter(amenity == "restaurant")

rest_now |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(cuisine)) |>
  separate_longer_delim(cuisine, delim = ";") |>
  mutate(cuisine = str_trim(str_to_lower(cuisine))) |>
  count(cuisine, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Cuisine", "Restaurants"))
Cuisine Restaurants
american 31
mexican 23
pizza 18
sandwich 13
asian 11
italian 10
japanese 10
burger 8
barbecue 7
breakfast 7 
scales::percent(mean(is.na(rest_now$cuisine)))   # share with no cuisine tag
# [1] "30%"

With that many missing, “Durham has few Thai restaurants” might only mean “few Thai restaurants are tagged.”

Comparing with Overture Maps

No single source of points of interest is complete, so it helps to compare OSM with an independent one. Overture Maps, backed by Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and TomTom, publishes an open places layer built from Facebook business pages, business registries, and Microsoft and Foursquare listings, not from OSM.

Overture releases are GeoParquet files in public cloud storage, with no API. The DuckDB database engine reads just the parts inside our bounding box, directly over the internet. Pinning the release date keeps the query reproducible while that release stays online.

library(duckdb)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())
invisible(dbExecute(con, "INSTALL spatial; LOAD spatial; INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs; SET s3_region = 'us-west-2';"))

ov_release <- "2026-10-21.0"   # see https://docs.overturemaps.org/release/latest/
ov_places  <- str_glue("s3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/{ov_release}/theme=places/type=place/*")

ov_sql <- str_glue("
  SELECT id, names.primary AS name, taxonomy.hierarchy AS hierarchy,
         confidence, operating_status, sources[1].dataset AS source,
         ST_AsText(geometry) AS geometry
  FROM read_parquet('{ov_places}')
  WHERE bbox.xmin > {durham_bb['x', 'min']} AND bbox.xmax < {durham_bb['x', 'max']}
    AND bbox.ymin > {durham_bb['y', 'min']} AND bbox.ymax < {durham_bb['y', 'max']}")

overture <- dbGetQuery(con, ov_sql) |>
  st_as_sf(wkt = "geometry", crs = 4326) |>   # keep the usual column name, so bind_rows() works later
  st_filter(durham)
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

nrow(overture)
# [1] 17457

The query takes seconds and returns every place in the city, from restaurants to dentists to churches. Where do they come from?

overture |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(source, sort = TRUE) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Source", "Places"))
Source Places
meta 8038
BrightQuery 4720
Microsoft 3210
Foursquare 1079
AllThePlaces 249
Uberall 72
DAC 65
PinMeTo 17
Birdeye 4
OpenTravel 2
RenderSEO 1

Each place also has a category hierarchy. Food places sit under food_and_drink:

is_food <- function(h) {          # h is one place's category hierarchy, e.g. c("food_and_drink", "restaurant")
  length(h) > 1 && h[1] == "food_and_drink"
}

overture_food <- overture |>
  filter(map_lgl(hierarchy, is_food)) |>
  mutate(category = map_chr(hierarchy, 2),
         amenity  = case_when(category == "restaurant"                   ~ "restaurant",
                              category == "casual_eatery"                ~ "fast_food",
                              category == "non_alcoholic_beverage_venue" ~ "cafe",
                              category == "alcoholic_beverage_venue"     ~ "bar or pub")) |>
  filter(!is.na(amenity))

The categories only roughly match OSM’s tags: “casual eatery” includes bakeries that OSM tags as shop, and Overture does not separate bars from pubs. Overture also has operating_status, which flags closed places, and confidence, its 0 to 1 estimate that a place exists. We keep open places with a confidence of at least 0.7.

ov <- overture_food |>
  filter(operating_status != "permanently_closed" | is.na(operating_status),
         confidence >= 0.7) |>
  select(ov_id = id, ov_name = name, amenity, confidence, source)

osm <- food |>
  mutate(amenity = if_else(amenity %in% c("bar", "pub"), "bar or pub", amenity)) |>
  filter(amenity != "food_court") |>
  select(osm_id, osm_name = name, amenity)

bind_rows(osm = st_drop_geometry(osm), overture = st_drop_geometry(ov), .id = "source") |>
  count(source, amenity) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = source, values_from = n) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Type", "OSM", "Overture"))
Type OSM Overture
bar or pub 44 124
cafe 41 89
fast_food 155 374
restaurant 272 771

Overture lists about 2.7 times as many places as OSM. Some of the gap is OSM missing businesses, especially new ones. Some is Overture’s noise: duplicates, stale listings and businesses filed in the wrong category, inherited from social media. Neither source is the truth; it is often best to triangulate from multiple sources.

Exercise 5: How much does confidence matter?

Recount Overture’s places by type with confidence thresholds of 0.5, 0.7 and 0.9. How much do the totals move? What does that say about any “number of restaurants” taken from a single source?

Solution 
count_at <- function(threshold) {
  overture_food |>
    st_drop_geometry() |>
    filter(operating_status != "permanently_closed" | is.na(operating_status),
           confidence >= threshold) |>
    count(amenity, name = paste("confidence ≥", threshold))
}

map(c(0.5, 0.7, 0.9), count_at) |>
  reduce(left_join, by = "amenity") |>
  knitr::kable()
amenity confidence ≥ 0.5 confidence ≥ 0.7 confidence ≥ 0.9
bar or pub 137 124 107
cafe 97 89 81
fast_food 409 374 317
restaurant 811 771 680

The count depends on a threshold someone chose. Any published number of restaurants rests on a similar choice, even when it is not visible.

Data that changes

OSM is edited thousands of times a minute. Running the same query next month will give a different answer, which is good for timeliness and bad for reproducibility. Overpass can, however, query OSM as it was on a past date, using the datetime argument. Here are Durham’s restaurants on the day this post was first published.

rest_2020 <- opq(durham_bb, timeout = 120, datetime = "2020-02-12T00:00:00Z") |>
  add_osm_feature(key = "amenity", value = "restaurant") |>
  get_osm() |>
  as_points() |>
  st_filter(durham)

rest_now <- food |> filter(amenity == "restaurant")

status <- full_join(
  rest_2020 |> st_drop_geometry() |> transmute(osm_id, in_2020 = TRUE),
  rest_now  |> st_drop_geometry() |> transmute(osm_id, in_now = TRUE),
  by = "osm_id") |>
  mutate(status = case_when(in_2020 & in_now ~ "in both",
                            is.na(in_now)    ~ "only in 2020",
                            is.na(in_2020)   ~ "only now"))
count(status, status) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("", "Restaurants"))
Restaurants
in both 147
only in 2020 38
only now 125

OSM had 185 restaurants in the city in February 2020 and has 272 now. Some of the change is real: restaurants open and close. Some of it is mapping: new restaurants are added long after they open, closed ones linger, and a restaurant redrawn from a point to a building outline gets a new osm_id even though nothing changed on the ground.

For reproducible work, record the date you downloaded the data, save the data you used, or query a fixed date with datetime, as above.

Conclusion

OSM is free, detailed and current. Using it well means crediting the contributors, being gentle with shared servers, checking the tags you rely on, and recording when you downloaded the data. Every points-of-interest dataset, OSM or Overture, reflects how it was collected.
